changes.before: Change the char initializer from single-quoted A to double-quoted A. What happens?
changes.after: Tell a single char value apart from a string of text.

before: A single-quoted literal such as 'A' is a char. Double quotes such as "Moon" form a string literal. They are not interchangeable types.
std::string, declared in <string>, stores a sequence of char values and manages its storage. std::string name{"Moon"} creates an owning string value.
name.size() reports its number of char units. This is not necessarily the number of visible Unicode symbols when text uses a multi-unit encoding.
A char variable accepts a character value such as 'B'. Assigning a whole double-quoted string literal to it is not a valid substitute.
Expected output or behavior: A 4. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Try a different single character and a different std::string. Explain the type difference rather than relying on their appearance when printed. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: char is a type that holds one small unit of character data. The ordinary letter 'A', written in single quotes, is a char value.
A string is a sequence of character units. std::string stores and manages that sequence for you. Include <string> to use it. Double quotes mark text such as "Moon".

name.size() counts the char units stored in name. For these simple English letters, each letter uses one unit. Some other characters use several units, so this is not always a count of visible letters.
Use single quotes for the one-letter char value in this example. A double-quoted string literal is a different type; C++ does not automatically turn it into a char.
The program prints A 4. mark supplies A. The single-quoted space separates the results. name.size() supplies 4 because Moon has four char units.
A string can contain one letter, many letters, or no letters. Even when it contains just one letter, it is still a string, not a char.

before.question: Change the char initializer from single-quoted A to double-quoted A. What happens?
choices: Compilation fails because the string literal is not a char value.
The string is automatically shortened to its first character.
before.explanation: Single and double quotes produce different kinds of values; the char variable cannot receive that string literal.

after.question: Change char mark{'A'} to char mark{"A"}. What happens?
choices: The two forms have the same type.
The compiler rejects the double-quoted text as a char initializer.
C++ automatically takes its first character.
after.explanation: Single-quoted 'A' is a char. Double-quoted "A" is a string literal, which cannot initialize this char.
